justification: Three of the writer's four claimed fixes are genuinely and cleanly done; the fourth introduces a new, checkable factual error that re-triggers the rubric's single-error cap, so the score stays at 7 despite real, verified progress. (1) The capping issue: I independently recomputed C(n) = 2(n+1)Hn - 4n in Node for n=100/1000/10000 and got 647.9/10985.9/155771.7, matching the article exactly; the stated percentages (2.6%/7.1%/6.0%) check out arithmetically against the article's own measured counts (631/10202/146439); and the exercise now explicitly cites the earlier 'shuffled first' quicksort-cost measurement (10,134 at n=1000, no median-of-three) as evidence the 20-30% headline was mostly the crude ~2n ln n baseline being loose, not median-of-three doing much -- the old causal overclaim is gone and the internal inconsistency round 1 flagged is now addressed head-on rather than papered over. (2) The un-wildcarded permutation counts: I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/algorithms/sorting-algorithms-compared.md` myself from PowerShell and got the same result the writer claims -- PASS, blocks=28, executed=14 -- which independently confirms min=12/max=17/average=15.7 are the program's real output, not asserted numbers. I separately recomputed the n=8 lower bound as ceil(log2(40320))=16 in Node, confirming the article's own 'lower bound, n=8: 16' line and its 'one comparison above the proven floor' claim are both correct and correctly scoped to n=8. (3) The quotation-casing fix: I pulled the live dotnet/runtime source directly (Array.cs line 23, ArraySortHelper.cs line 186 and duplicates) and confirmed the originals read 'Empirically, 16 seems to speed up...' and 'Compute median-of-three.  But also partition them...' (capital E, capital C) -- the article's '[e]mpirically' and '[c]ompute' correctly bracket the altered-case initial letter per standard mid-sentence-quotation convention. (Trivial, non-scored nit: the source has two spaces after 'median-of-three.' and the article normalizes to one; this is ordinary whitespace collapsing, not a misquote.) (4) The toolchain statement: present, accurate-sounding, and -- checked against where sibling AdSense articles place theirs (big-o-notation.md:292, value-types-vs-reference-types.md:306, garbage-collection.md:232, processes-and-threads.md:259, arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md:62) -- correctly placed as prose beside the first block with a real seeded measurement (quicksort-cost) rather than stamped into the opening paragraph, matching editorial brief rule 30 and the house style. But the second sentence of that same addition is wrong: 'Random's algorithm changed in .NET 6, so a reader on an older major version would see different ... numbers from the same seed' is uncited and, on primary-source verification, backwards for exactly the usage on this page. Microsoft's own .NET 6 performance devblog (Stephen Toub, 'Performance Improvements in .NET 6') states explicitly that the .NET 6 algorithm change applies only to the unseeded `new Random()` case, and that the team deliberately kept the old, decades-old algorithm for `new Random(seed)` specifically to avoid changing numeric sequences from a fixed seed ('we fall back to the old implementation if a seed is supplied, otherwise preferring the new algorithm'). I confirmed this is still true in the current dotnet/runtime main branch: Random.cs's `Random(int Seed)` constructor routes to `CompatSeedImpl(Seed)` for the base `Random` type. Every seeded-Random block on this page -- Random(1), Random(2), Random(3), Random(5), Random(7), Random(11) -- uses exactly this constructor form, so a reader on .NET 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10 would get the identical comparison counts shown in the article, not different ones; nothing about these particular integer comparison counts is actually version-dependent. This is a new, checkable, uncited factual claim (violating editorial brief rule 3, which requires a primary source for every non-obvious factual claim) introduced by this round's own fix, and per the rubric a single factual error caps the technical score at 7 -- the same mechanism that capped round 1, now triggered by a different sentence in the same area of the article. Rest of the independent pass: `run-code.mjs` passed exactly as claimed; I re-verified the Array.Sort documentation bullets (16-element insertion-sort cutoff, 2*Log N heapsort trigger, Quicksort otherwise, 'O(n log n) operation') against the live learn.microsoft.com page and they are unchanged and accurate; I re-derived every complexity claim in the article (insertion sort n-1/n(n-1)/2, selection sort n(n-1)/2 fixed, merge sort's [n log2 n / 2, n log2 n] bound for n=8 giving [12,24], quicksort's ~2n ln n average and Theta(n^2) worst case, heap sort's <2n lg n bound, and the ceil(log2(n!)) decision-tree floor including the n=5/n=6 exercise values 7 and 10) and found all of them correct. `docs/crosslinks/algorithms/sorting-algorithms-compared.md` now exists with sensible entries, resolving round 1's minor crosslinks finding as a bonus (not one of the four claimed fixes, but verified present and correctly scoped per the editorial brief's crosslink rule). No other new technical errors were found in the sections touched this round. With the Random-algorithm sentence corrected or removed, this article has no known technical defects left and would credibly clear 9+.

issues.problem: The toolchain statement itself is accurate and well-placed (matches where sibling articles state theirs, beside the first real measurement rather than in the opening paragraph). But the causal claim attached to it is wrong for the exact case it's describing. Microsoft's official .NET 6 performance blog post (Stephen Toub) states the new Random algorithm in .NET 6 applies only to the unseeded `new Random()` case; for `new Random(seed)`, the runtime deliberately falls back to the old, pre-.NET-6 algorithm specifically so fixed-seed sequences would not change -- 'we fall back to the old implementation if a seed is supplied, otherwise preferring the new algorithm.' I confirmed this compat behavior is still present in the current dotnet/runtime main branch (Random.cs, `Random(int Seed)` routes to `CompatSeedImpl`). Every seeded-Random usage on this page (Random(1), Random(2), Random(3), Random(5), Random(7), Random(11)) uses this exact constructor form, so a reader on .NET 5 through .NET 10 (and arguably .NET Framework) would see the *same* comparison counts from the same seed, not different ones. The claim is also uncited, which independently violates the editorial brief's rule that every non-obvious factual claim needs a primary source cited inline.
